title: Functional Model in Depth
description: The functional model organizes the entire company around specialties, and its depth repays study because most companies start here. Structure: C-level functional heads (CTO, CMO, CFO, COO) each owning their people, budgets, and standards; the CEO integrates. Coordination mechanisms: the product manager or program manager as the cross-functional glue, weekly cross-functional councils, and shared planning cycles. Variants: the strong-functional (powerful functional heads, weak product roles — deep expertise, slow products) versus the product-weighted functional (strong product managers — Apple’s famous model, where functions serve products). Apple’s functional organization under Jobs and Cook is the exemplar: world-class functional experts (design, engineering) coordinated by strong product leadership, producing integrated products no divisional structure could. The model breaks when products need genuinely different things from the same function — the enterprise product and the consumer product fighting over one engineering org — which is when companies add divisions or business units.
key_points: C-level functional heads; CEO integrates
Coordination via product/program roles and councils
Apple’s product-weighted functional as exemplar
Breaks when products need different things from one function
core_principles: Functions serve products (or vice versa — choose)
how_it_works: Functional heads own people and standards; product roles coordinate across; planning cycles synchronize; CEO resolves conflicts.
watch_outs: Product needs fighting over shared functions
best_fit: Single-product or integrated-product companies.

title: Product-Unit (Divisional) Model in Depth
description: The product-unit model gives each major product its own mini-company, and its economics deserve the deep look. Each unit carries full P&L: revenue, cost, headcount, and investment authority within corporate guardrails. The corporate center’s value-add must be explicit and measured — shared services at market-beating cost, capital allocation smarter than the market, capability building (leadership, technology) the units cannot do alone — because the center’s cost is visible and resented otherwise. Transfer pricing between units (one unit’s component in another’s product) is the perennial friction; the rule is market-based pricing with arbitration, not cost-plus politics. Portfolio logic governs: invest in stars, harvest cash cows, fix or exit dogs — the BCG matrix as capital allocation discipline. The model’s test: can the company kill a failing unit? If not, the P&L accountability is theater. Exemplars: GE’s business units (Welch era), Alphabet’s Other Bets structure.
key_points: Full P&L per unit within corporate guardrails
Corporate center must earn its keep explicitly
Transfer pricing: market-based with arbitration
Test: can the company kill a failing unit?
how_it_works: Units operate as mini-companies; corporate allocates capital, sets guardrails, provides shared services; portfolio reviewed yearly.
best_fit: Multi-product companies with distinct markets.

title: Geographic Divisional Model
description: The geographic model divides the company by region — Americas, EMEA, APAC, or country-level — each with its own P&L and leadership, and it exists because markets differ by regulation, culture, language, and competition. The regional head owns go-to-market, partnerships, and regulatory relationships; product development usually stays global (or regionalizes where required — China’s tech stack being the extreme case). The design tension is global consistency versus local adaptation: brand and core product stay global, pricing/packaging/partnerships localize. Matrix overlays are common — regional sales reporting to both the regional head and the global sales function. The model’s failure mode is the “barony”: regions optimizing locally at global cost (divergent products, channel conflicts). The counter is global product authority with regional commercial authority — products global, go-to-market local. Exemplars: consumer goods multinationals (P&G, Unilever), whose regional structures are a century old.
key_points: Regions own P&L, go-to-market, regulatory relationships
Products usually global; commercial usually local
Tension: global consistency vs local adaptation
Barony risk: regions optimizing at global cost
core_principles: Markets differ; organize for the difference
how_it_works: Regional heads own commercial results; global functions own product and brand; matrix reporting on shared functions; yearly region reviews.
best_fit: Multinationals in regulation- or culture-differentiated markets.

title: Customer-Segment Model
description: The customer-segment model organizes around who buys — enterprise, SMB, consumer; or by industry vertical — because different customers buy differently. Enterprise segments need field sales, solution engineering, and long cycles; SMB needs inside sales and self-serve; consumer needs brand and retail. Each segment gets its own go-to-market, its own P&L, and often its own product variants. The model’s power is commercial focus: the enterprise team learns enterprise buying, undistracted by consumer campaigns. The cost is product fragmentation — three segments pulling the product three ways — managed by a strong product organization with segment input but global product authority. Pricing and packaging differ per segment (the same core at different value metrics), which the segment teams own. The model fits companies whose segments genuinely differ in buying behavior; where they do not, it is just expensive duplication. Exemplars: Microsoft’s enterprise/SMB/consumer splits, banks’ retail/commercial/wealth divisions.
key_points: Organized by buyer: enterprise, SMB, consumer, verticals
Each segment: own GTM, P&L, product variants
Power: commercial focus per buying behavior
Product stays global; segments advise
core_principles: Sell the way each segment buys
how_it_works: Segment GMs own commercial results; global product builds with segment input; pricing/packaging per segment; segment P&Ls reviewed.
watch_outs: Expensive if segments do not truly differ
best_fit: Companies with genuinely different buyer behaviors.

title: Strong vs Weak Matrix
description: Not all matrices are equal: the strong-weak axis decides who really decides. In a strong matrix, the project/product manager controls budget and priorities — functional managers supply people and standards but do not override project decisions (aerospace programs, construction). In a weak matrix, functional managers dominate and project managers coordinate without authority — the “project coordinator” model. The balanced matrix splits authority, requiring genuine negotiation. The choice follows the work: strong matrix where project success dominates (complex deliverables, deadlines), weak where functional excellence dominates (research, professional services), balanced where both matter equally. The failure is mismatch — a strong-matrix project run by a weak-matrix coordinator, or vice versa — which produces the worst of both: confusion plus powerlessness. Document which matrix you run, per project type, and staff the project manager’s authority to match. The matrix’s reputation for dysfunction comes mostly from undeclared strength.
key_points: Strong: project manager controls budget and priority
Weak: functional managers dominate; PM coordinates
Balanced: genuine negotiation required
Match strength to the work; document it
core_principles: Staff PM authority to the declared strength
how_it_works: Classify project types by needed strength, assign PM authority accordingly, document in the project charter, review fit yearly.
best_fit: Project organizations with varied project types.

title: The Platform Operating Model
description: The platform model organizes the company as an ecosystem: a core platform team builds shared capabilities (infrastructure, data, identity, payments), and product or business teams build on top. Technology companies made it canonical — Amazon’s platform teams, Google’s infrastructure — but the logic is general: shared capabilities get platform-grade investment once instead of being rebuilt N times. The design rules: the platform is a product with customers (the internal teams) — it needs product management, SLAs, and a roadmap, not a ticket queue; adoption is earned through quality, with mandates only where justified (security, compliance); and the platform charges back or is funded centrally — free platforms get abused, taxed platforms get bypassed. Conway’s law runs in reverse here: the platform’s APIs shape what product teams can build, so platform design is product strategy. The failure mode is the ivory-tower platform — built without customers, adopted by none. Best fit: companies with multiple products sharing deep capabilities.
key_points: Core platform teams build shared capabilities
Platform as product: PM, SLAs, roadmap — not a ticket queue
Adoption earned; mandates only where justified
Platform APIs shape product strategy
how_it_works: Platform teams ship versioned capabilities with SLAs; product teams build on them; funding via chargeback or central; adoption reviewed.
best_fit: Multi-product companies with deep shared capabilities.

title: The Network / Ecosystem Model
description: The network model extends the company beyond its payroll: orchestrating an ecosystem of partners, developers, suppliers, and even customers who create value together. Apple’s App Store, Amazon’s marketplace, and Salesforce’s partner ecosystem are the exemplars — the company owns the platform and the rules, the network provides the variety. The operating disciplines differ from internal management: governance by terms and APIs rather than hierarchy, incentives by revenue share rather than salary, quality by review and ratings rather than supervision. The orchestrator’s jobs: keep the platform attractive (tools, economics, audience), keep the rules fair and stable (rule changes are the ecosystem’s earthquakes), and manage the “platform vs participant” tension (when the orchestrator competes with its own network). The model’s economics are powerful — the network’s innovation exceeds any single company’s — and its risks are systemic: the ecosystem’s failures become the orchestrator’s. Best fit: companies whose value grows with participant variety.
key_points: Orchestrate ecosystems beyond the payroll
Governance by terms and APIs, not hierarchy
Platform vs participant tension is permanent
Network innovation exceeds any single company
core_principles: The ecosystem’s success is the product
Stable fair rules; changes are earthquakes
how_it_works: Build the platform, set terms and APIs, attract participants, govern by review and rules, share economics, manage tensions.
best_fit: Platforms whose value grows with participant variety.

title: The Franchise Model
description: The franchise model scales through owner-operators: the franchisor owns the brand, systems, and supply chain; franchisees own the outlets, invest the capital, and run the operations. McDonald’s perfected it — 95% of restaurants franchised — proving the model scales faster on other people’s capital with operators who have skin in the game. The operating system is the franchise agreement plus the operations manual: site selection, build-out specs, training, approved suppliers, marketing funds, and quality audits — the manual is the OS, often thousands of pages. The franchisor’s disciplines: select franchisees rigorously (the operator matters more than the location), enforce standards consistently (the audit program is the brand’s immune system), and innovate centrally while letting operators adapt locally. The tensions are structural: franchisor’s brand control vs franchisee’s autonomy, royalty economics, and renewal/territory disputes. Best fit: replicable local operations — food, fitness, services, retail.
key_points: Franchisor: brand and systems; franchisee: capital and operations
The operations manual is the OS
Select operators rigorously; audit consistently
Scales on franchisees’ capital with skin in the game
core_principles: Operators’ success is the system’s success
how_it_works: Franchisor documents the system, selects and trains operators, supplies the chain, audits quality; franchisees invest and operate.
best_fit: Replicable local operations: food, fitness, services.

title: The Holding Company Model
description: The holding company owns businesses and allocates capital but does not operate them: Berkshire Hathaway is the archetype — dozens of businesses run by their own CEOs, Omaha providing capital allocation, culture, and permanent ownership. The model’s operating system is minimal by design: acquire good businesses with good managers, do not interfere, allocate the cash flows to the best opportunities, and measure by return on capital over decades. The disciplines are selection (buy right — the model cannot fix a bad business), manager retention (autonomy and trust keep the operators), and capital allocation (the holding company’s true skill — moving cash from cash cows to opportunities). The model fails when the holding company cannot resist meddling, or when it overpays — there is no operational value-add to compensate. Variants: the conglomerate (more operational involvement), the family office holding, the search-fund portfolio. Best fit: capital allocators with selection skill and permanent horizons.
key_points: Owns businesses; allocates capital; does not operate
OS is minimal: buy right, do not interfere, allocate cash
Disciplines: selection, retention, allocation
Fails on meddling or overpaying
how_it_works: Acquire good businesses with good managers, grant autonomy, sweep and reallocate cash flows, measure ROIC over decades.
watch_outs: No operational fix for bad buys
best_fit: Capital allocators with selection skill.

title: The Cooperative / Employee-Owned Model
description: Cooperatives and employee-owned companies (Mondragon’s 80,000 worker-owners, John Lewis Partnership, US ESOPs) organize around member ownership: the workers (or customers, in consumer co-ops) own the company and elect its governance. The operating model replaces shareholder primacy with member benefit — profits distribute as patronage or wages, strategy serves the members’ long-term interests. Governance: one member one vote (co-ops) or trust-held shares with employee voice (ESOPs, John Lewis’s partnership council). The disciplines: member education (owners must understand the business), democratic process that still decides (representative structures, not every decision by referendum), and capital discipline (co-ops cannot easily raise equity — they retain earnings or borrow). Performance data surprises skeptics: employee-owned firms show higher productivity and resilience in downturns (lower layoffs, shared sacrifice). The model’s cost is decision speed and capital access. Best fit: businesses where workforce stability and mission alignment are strategic.
key_points: Members own; one member one vote (or trust-held)
Profits to members; strategy serves long-term interests
Disciplines: member education, workable democracy, capital care
Higher productivity and downturn resilience documented
core_principles: Long-term member benefit over quarterly extraction
how_it_works: Members elect governance, share profits, participate through representative structures, fund growth via retained earnings.
best_fit: Businesses where workforce stability is strategic.

title: The Studio / Partnership Model
description: Professional partnerships (law, consulting, accounting, architecture) and studios organize around partners who own the firm and the craft: the partnership track (associate to partner) is the operating system’s spine. Economics: leverage — partners’ judgment sold at high rates, delivered partly by associates at lower cost — with the pyramid’s shape set by the work’s complexity. Governance: partners vote on major decisions (admitting partners, mergers, compensation systems — lockstep vs eat-what-you-kill); managing partners administer. The disciplines: the partnership admission (up-or-out or permanent senior roles — the choice shapes culture for decades), client ownership (institutional vs partner-held), and knowledge management (the firm’s methods must outlive individuals). The model’s tensions: short-term partner distributions vs long-term investment, stars vs institution, growth vs selectivity. Variants: the design studio (principal-led, craft-first), the agency holding model. Best fit: expertise businesses where judgment is the product.
key_points: Partners own; partnership track is the spine
Economics: leverage of judgment over delivery cost
Governance: partner votes on major decisions
Tensions: distributions vs investment, stars vs institution
how_it_works: Associates deliver, partners sell and judge, partnership admits owners, profits distribute by formula, knowledge systematized.
best_fit: Expertise businesses: law, consulting, design, accounting.

title: The Ambidextrous Organization
description: The ambidextrous organization runs two operating models at once: exploit (the core business, optimized for efficiency) and explore (new ventures, optimized for learning) — because the disciplines contradict and one model cannot serve both. O’Reilly and Tushman’s research shows ambidextrous firms outperform in turbulent industries. The design: structural separation (the explore unit has its own P&L, metrics, and processes — not the core’s stage-gates), senior-team integration (the top team manages the tension and allocates between horizons), and distinct metrics (core: margin and efficiency; explore: learning velocity and option value). The failure mode is contamination — the core’s processes, metrics, and antibodies killing the explore unit — which is why separation must be real (different building helps) and the CEO must visibly protect it. The return path matters too: successful explores get integrated without being smothered. Best fit: incumbents facing disruption who cannot afford to bet the core or ignore the future.
key_points: Exploit and explore need contradictory disciplines
Structural separation with senior-team integration
Distinct metrics: efficiency vs learning velocity
Protect the explore unit from core antibodies
core_principles: One model cannot serve both horizons
The top team holds the tension
how_it_works: Separate explore units with own P&L and metrics; senior team allocates across horizons; integrate successes carefully.
best_fit: Incumbents facing disruption.

title: The Conglomerate Model
description: The conglomerate — unrelated businesses under one corporate roof (the classic GE, 3M’s diversified industrials) — exists for capital allocation, shared capabilities, and risk diversification. The operating model: business units with full P&L, corporate providing capital, leadership development, and select shared functions (treasury, audit, sometimes R&D). The conglomerate’s historical logic (1960s–80s): internal capital markets beat external ones, diversification smooths cycles, and professional management transfers across industries. The modern critique: the conglomerate discount (markets value the parts above the whole), complexity costs, and the evidence that focus beats breadth — driving the great de-conglomeration (GE’s breakup, Siemens’ spin-offs). Survivors’ disciplines: ruthless portfolio review (fix, sell, or close), genuine capability sharing (not just shared letterhead), and honest conglomerate-premium math. The model persists where capabilities truly transfer (3M’s materials science across divisions) or capital access truly advantages (Berkshire-style). Best fit: diversified capability or capital advantages that survive honest math.
key_points: Unrelated businesses; corporate allocates capital and talent
Historical logic: internal capital markets, diversification
Modern pressure: conglomerate discount, de-conglomeration wave
Survives where capabilities or capital truly transfer
core_principles: Portfolio discipline: fix, sell, or close
how_it_works: Units run P&Ls; corporate allocates capital, develops leaders, shares real capabilities; portfolio reviewed ruthlessly.
best_fit: Genuine capability or capital advantages across units.

title: The Keiretsu / Chaebol Network Model
description: East Asia’s network models — Japan’s keiretsu (Mitsubishi, Mitsui groups) and Korea’s chaebol (Samsung, Hyundai) — organize as affiliated company networks bound by cross-shareholding, history, and coordination rather than single ownership. The keiretsu’s horizontal groups share a main bank, trading company, and presidents’ council; vertical keiretsu organize supply chains (Toyota’s suppliers). Chaebol concentrate family control across dozens of affiliates. The operating advantages: patient capital (main-bank relationships through cycles), supply-chain coordination (Toyota’s just-in-time needed keiretsu trust), and long-horizon investment. The pathologies: tunneling (controlling families extracting via related-party deals), zombie affiliates kept alive by group support, and governance opacity — Korea’s chaebol reforms target exactly these. The model’s lesson for Western managers: trust-based coordination can outperform contracts where relationships are long — and entrench insiders where accountability is weak. Best fit: economies with relationship capitalism and patient capital.
key_points: Affiliated networks bound by cross-shareholding and history
Advantages: patient capital, supply-chain trust, long horizons
Pathologies: tunneling, zombies, opacity
Trust outperforms contracts where relationships are long
how_it_works: Affiliates coordinate via councils, banks, and trading companies; cross-shareholding stabilizes; families/groups steer strategy.
best_fit: Relationship-capitalism economies.

title: The Virtual / Hollow Corporation
description: The virtual corporation (the “hollow” model — Nike’s famous formulation) owns the brand, design, and marketing while outsourcing manufacturing, logistics, and often everything physical to a network of contractors. The operating model is orchestration: the company’s core competencies are design, brand, and supply-chain management; everything else is contracted. The disciplines: supplier selection and development (the contractors’ capabilities are your capabilities), quality systems extending into suppliers’ factories, supply-chain visibility (multi-tier mapping — the factory’s factory), and the ethics audit function (labor and environmental standards, because the brand owns the scandal). The model’s economics: asset-light scaling, variable costs, focus on the high-margin layers. The risks: supply-chain fragility (learned painfully in 2020–22), quality distance, and the knowledge drain — outsource manufacturing long enough and you forget how things are made. Best fit: brand-and-design companies in modular industries.
key_points: Own brand, design, marketing; outsource the physical
Core competence is orchestration
Disciplines: supplier development, visibility, ethics audits
Risks: fragility, quality distance, knowledge drain
how_it_works: Design and brand in-house; contract manufacturing and logistics; manage via quality systems, visibility, and audits.
best_fit: Brand/design companies in modular industries.

title: Choosing an Operating Model
description: Operating model selection is the highest-leverage org design decision, and the method is analytical, not fashionable. Step one: name the strategy’s demands — what must the organization do excellently (innovate? execute efficiently? serve segments? scale fast?). Step two: map the work’s nature — project vs process, expertise depth vs breadth, market similarity vs difference. Step three: shortlist models that fit (functional for depth, divisional for distinct markets, matrix for projects, platform for shared capabilities, network for ecosystems). Step four: test the shortlist against the failure modes — every model’s pathology will visit you; pick the pathology you can manage. Step five: design the seams — decision rights, coordination mechanisms, metrics — because models fail at the interfaces. The review trigger: when the strategy changes, the market shifts, or the model’s pathology dominates the conversation, revisit. The meta-rule: no perfect model exists — only the model whose trade-offs fit your strategy and whose failure modes you govern.
key_points: Analytical selection: strategy demands, work nature, fit
Test shortlists against failure modes
Design the seams: rights, coordination, metrics
No perfect model — only managed trade-offs
core_principles: Pick the pathology you can manage
how_it_works: Assess demands, map work, shortlist, stress-test, design seams, install, review on strategy or market change.
best_fit: Any organization choosing or changing its model.

title: Functional Model: Coordination Mechanisms
description: Functional models live or die by their coordination mechanisms — the explicit systems that move work across silos. The product manager (or program manager) is the primary mechanism: a role with cross-functional authority over the product’s priorities, negotiating with functional heads for resources. Cross-functional councils (weekly product councils, launch committees) synchronize at leadership level. Shared planning cycles (quarterly planning with cross-functional dependencies mapped) prevent the “surprise dependency” failure. Liaison roles and rotation programs build the informal networks that actually move work — the engineer who did a marketing rotation gets answers faster. The metrics must be shared: when engineering is measured on velocity and sales on revenue with no shared product metric, the functions optimize locally. The coordination budget is real — expect 10–20% of senior time in cross-functional work — and under-budgeting it is the classic functional failure. Design the mechanisms deliberately; the silos are structural, so the bridges must be too.
key_points: Product/program managers as cross-functional glue
Councils, shared planning, liaison rotations
Shared metrics prevent local optimization
Budget 10–20% of senior time for coordination
core_principles: Silos are structural; bridges must be deliberate
how_it_works: Install product roles, councils, and planning cycles; set shared metrics; fund the coordination time explicitly.
strengths: Keeps functional depth while moving work
best_fit: Functional organizations above ~100 people.

title: Divisional Model: Shared Services Design
description: Divisions duplicate functions unless shared services are designed deliberately — and shared services fail unless designed as internal businesses. The design decisions: which services share (finance, HR, IT infrastructure, legal — the scale-advantaged) versus which stay divisional (sales ops, product-adjacent engineering). The service model: the shared center operates with SLAs, chargeback or allocation pricing, and divisional choice where feasible — captive monopolies breed resentment and bloat. Governance: a services board with divisional representation sets priorities and rates. The failure modes: the “corporate tax” perception (divisions seeing only cost, not value), the one-size-fits-none standard (enterprise IT strangling a nimble division), and the shadow-function response (divisions rebuilding what shared services do badly). The test: would divisions buy this service voluntarily? If not, fix the service or release the function. Well-run shared services are a conglomerate advantage; badly run ones are the first thing activists target.
key_points: Share scale-advantaged services; keep product-adjacent local
Run shared services as internal businesses: SLAs, pricing, choice
Governance via divisional-represented services board
Test: would divisions buy voluntarily?
how_it_works: Classify services, stand up SLA-based shared centers, price transparently, govern jointly, review the buy-voluntarily test yearly.
best_fit: Divisional companies with duplicable functions.

title: Matrix Model: Decision Rights Design
description: The matrix works when decision rights are explicit and fails when they are tribal. The design tool is the decision matrix: rows are recurring decisions (hire, budget, priority, scope, launch), columns are the two axes (functional, project), cells name the decider and the consulted. The rules: one decider per cell (never joint — joint means deadlock), escalation paths with time limits (disagreements resolve in days, not quarters), and a standing “matrix council” for the decisions the matrix did not anticipate. Staffing matters equally: matrix managers need collaborative skill and comfort with shared authority — the brilliant authoritarian fails here. The launch discipline: train both axes in the decision matrix before go-live, run the first quarter’s conflicts as calibration, and publish the precedents. The maintenance: review the matrix on every reorganization, because new leaders inherit old ambiguities otherwise. Explicit rights turn the matrix from blame-generator into flexibility engine.
key_points: Decision matrix: decisions x axes, one decider per cell
Escalation paths with time limits
Staff for collaborative skill
Review on every reorganization
how_it_works: Build the decision matrix, train both axes, run calibration quarter, publish precedents, review on reorg.
best_fit: Matrix organizations of any scale.

title: Platform Model: Platform Product Management
description: Platform teams fail when run as ticket queues and succeed when run as products — platform product management is the discipline. The platform PM’s customers are internal product teams; the job is roadmapping capabilities they will want, with the same discovery rigor as external product (interviews, usage data, beta programs). The SLA is the contract: uptime, latency, support response — published and measured, because product teams bet their launches on the platform. Versioning and deprecation policy are the trust infrastructure: breaking changes announced quarters ahead, migration tooling provided, never surprise deprecations. Adoption metrics replace ticket counts: which teams use which capabilities, satisfaction scores, time-to-first-success for new teams. Funding follows value: chargeback/showback makes costs visible, central funding for true commons (security, identity). The platform PM’s hardest job is saying no — every team wants custom features; the platform stays coherent by building the common 80% brilliantly.
key_points: Platform as product: discovery, roadmap, SLAs
Versioning and deprecation policy as trust infrastructure
Adoption metrics over ticket counts
Say no to custom; build the common 80%
how_it_works: PM discovers needs, roadmaps capabilities, publishes SLAs, versions carefully, measures adoption, funds transparently.
strengths: Platform teams ship what teams need
best_fit: Companies running platform models.

title: Network Model: Ecosystem Governance
description: Ecosystem governance is regulation without government: the orchestrator sets the rules the network lives by. The instruments: terms of service and developer agreements (the constitution), API versioning and deprecation policy (the stability promise), review and certification (the quality gate), revenue share (the economics), and dispute resolution (the courts). The governance disciplines: change management — rule changes announced early, migrated gradually, never retroactive punishment; consistency — rules applied to the orchestrator’s own products too (the Apple-Spotify tension is the cautionary tale); and voice — advisory councils and transparent roadmaps that give participants predictability. The failure modes: capricious enforcement (rules as weapons), rent extraction (raising the take until the ecosystem withers), and self-preferencing (the platform competing with participants using insider data). The healthy ecosystem’s test: do participants invest long-term? Investment follows trusted governance. The orchestrator’s paradox: the power to change the rules is the reason participants fear you — constrain it visibly.
key_points: Instruments: terms, APIs, review, revenue share, disputes
Change management: early, gradual, never retroactive
Consistency: rules bind the orchestrator too
Participants invest where governance is trusted
how_it_works: Publish terms and APIs, version carefully, review consistently, share economics fairly, resolve disputes transparently, evolve rules gradually.
best_fit: Ecosystem orchestrators.

title: Hybrid Models in Practice
description: Real companies run hybrids — pure models are textbook cases. The common hybrids: functional core with divisional overlays (product divisions drawing on shared functions), matrix by exception (functional normally, matrix for big programs), platform plus product teams (the tech standard), geographic plus product matrix (multinationals), franchise plus corporate stores (retail). The design discipline for hybrids: name the primary model (the one that governs headcount, budgets, and careers — ambiguity here breeds politics), define the secondary model’s scope explicitly (which decisions, which units), and design the interfaces between them (who resolves primary-vs-secondary conflicts). The hybrid’s failure mode is undeclared hybridity — the company that is “functional” on paper but runs shadow divisions, creating two org charts and zero clarity. The honest org chart shows the hybrid as it is. The review question: does each part of the hybrid earn its complexity? Simplify where the answer is no.
key_points: Pure models are textbook; hybrids are reality
Name the primary model explicitly
Define secondary scope and interface conflicts
Undeclared hybridity creates two org charts, zero clarity
core_principles: Primary model governs careers and budgets
how_it_works: Map the actual model, name primary and secondaries, design interfaces, publish the honest chart, simplify yearly.
best_fit: Real companies above ~200 people.

title: Operating Model Transitions
description: Changing operating models is organizational surgery — necessary periodically, dangerous always. The triggers: strategy change (new markets need new models), scale thresholds (the functional model breaking at 300), performance crisis (the model’s pathology dominating), or M&A (two models colliding). The method: diagnose first (is the model the problem, or leadership, or strategy?), design the target with the seams specified, pilot where possible (one division, one region), sequence the change (structure, then decision rights, then metrics, then systems — people need the new logic in order), and over-communicate the why (the narrative carries people through the discomfort). The timeline: 12–24 months for enterprise model changes; faster breaks things, slower loses momentum. The people dimension: some leaders thrive in the new model and some do not — assess honestly and transition kindly but firmly. The success metric: the new model’s intended behaviors appearing without enforcement.
key_points: Triggers: strategy, scale, crisis, M&A
Sequence: structure, rights, metrics, systems
12–24 months enterprise; faster breaks, slower stalls
Success: intended behaviors without enforcement
how_it_works: Diagnose, design with seams, pilot, sequence, communicate relentlessly, assess leaders, measure behaviors.
best_fit: Companies outgrowing or out-strategizing their model.

title: The One-Page Operating Model Canvas
description: The operating model canvas compresses the design onto one page so leadership can see, debate, and align on it. The blocks: value proposition (what the company promises customers), key capabilities (what it must do excellently), structure (the org model — functional, divisional, matrix), decision rights (who decides the recurring big calls), core processes (the 6–10 that run the business), cadence (the meeting and planning rhythms), metrics (the scorecard), culture and principles (the decision rules), and talent (the hiring bar and key roles). The canvas’s use: fill it in a leadership workshop, argue the trade-offs block by block, and publish the result — the one-page OS the whole company can learn. The review: revisit when strategy shifts or the company doubles. The canvas’s power is forcing completeness — the blank “decision rights” block reveals the gap every org chart hides. One page, nine blocks, the whole system visible.
key_points: Nine blocks: value to talent on one page
Workshop tool: fill, argue, publish
Forces completeness — blank blocks reveal gaps
Revisit on strategy shift or doubling
core_principles: One page the company can learn
how_it_works: Leadership workshops the canvas block by block, publishes the one-pager, teaches it in onboarding, reviews on change.
best_fit: Leadership teams designing or aligning on their OS.
